narrative:
The model predicts you have a 25% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to strengthen your performance before it’s too late.

The three factors that most influenced this decision were your past academic failures, your reason for choosing this school, and your ambition to pursue higher education. Having already failed one class previously was the strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. While most students who passed had zero prior failures, your history of one failure signaled to the model a pattern that increases the risk of not passing this year.

Your reason for selecting this school—being close to home—worked in the opposite direction and pulled the prediction toward passing. This choice is less common among successful students, who more often picked the school for its course offerings or reputation, yet the model still saw it as a mild positive factor for you.

Wanting to continue into higher education was the third most important element and also pushed the prediction toward passing. Every student who ultimately passed shared this same strong ambition, so the model viewed your goal as a clear protective factor.

To improve, focus first on breaking the cycle of past failures by creating a consistent study routine and seeking help early. Even though you currently study less than two hours per week—far below the 2–5 hours that most successful students dedicate—small, regular increases in study time, combined with reducing your unusually high number of absences (average among passers is under 4), can meaningfully raise your chances.
